speechtext: On the Orders of the Day being called,

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I de-s're to draw the attention of the House to
an item which appears iu this morning's ' Citizen.' I took the liberty of notifying the Minister of Militia this morning of the item and of asking him to look into it. The item reads as follows :
London, Ontario, June 11-(Special).-As the by-election here on Tuesday is likely to be close, whichever way it goes, the government is putting forth every effort to deter Conservative voters from exercising their franchise on Tuesday next. The latest scheme has been worked through the Militia Department. Six soldiers at tVolseley barracks have suddenly been ordered to report for duty at Niagara tomorrow. Every man of the six is a Conservative, and there is naturally a deal of indignation among Mr. Gray's friends at this mean political move on the part of the militia authorities.
I have not any further evidence before me than what is contained iu this item ; the facts are, though, that there is at the present time a camp in the city of Loudon, aud one would naturally suppose that this is the camp where these soldiers would be employed. The headquarters in Toronto for the permanent force is the source from which instructors would usually be drawn for Niagara. It may be stated that some of the soldiers from Toronto have been drafted away to Halifax to form a garrison there, and that therefore the London camp must be called upon to furnish men for certain duties at Niagara, but the fact stands forth that the camp at Niagara does not open until to-morrow, the date of the election, and the troops will not reach Niagara until tomorrow night. Therefore, there was no necessity, under any consideration whatever, to order these men from London before they had an opportunity of casting their ballots in the election to-morrow, whichever way they cast them. It does not matter to me how they vote, but they should have had this privilege, and then they could be in camp at Niagara to-morrow night in ample time for any instructional duties they may be called on to perform. Thg camp will not begin instructional work until Wednesday at the earliest. I trust the minister will be able to let us have full information in connection with this matter. It must be borne in mind that although these men are members of the permanent corps they lose none of their rights as citizens, that a soldier has every right which is possessed by any other citizen, and he should have his franchise the same as if he were an ordinary citizen. For some reason or other, the permanent corps, although the wages paid are high, as the rate has been increased, is not kept up to the establishment at all ; they are several hundred, I believe, short of the establishment at the present time.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext:
Although the pay is better than the men would get in the ordinary walks of life. The minister will

be able to tell what tbe situation is. While explaining this matter, the minister might take the opportunity of explaining some correspondence which I understand he had with the Liberal candidate in Toronto in relation to the increased pay of the soldiers on the eve of the last election. It is very strange that this correspondence should take place between the minister and an ordinary candidate, but perhaps the minister knows nothing about this London affair ; it may be another case of the Minister of Agriculture and the Eastern Townships-that he is the minister of the district ; it may be that this time the minister of the district of London is exercising his functions in sending these men off without the authority of the minister. My object in speaking to the minister this morning primarily was that he might take some steps so that the men might not leave London until to-morrow. The train leaves in the afternoon in plenty of time for them to reach Niagara in the evening. If the men who are taken must be Conservatives, I take that as a compliment. The great majority of the men in the militia are Conservatives, and when they are selected as instructors I venture to say the great majority will still be Conservatives, because they have always been found to be tbe most Intelligent men in the militia.

speechtext: That seems to be peculiar to the force, not to the rest of the community.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext:
Although I take it as quite a compliment to the force that the Conservatives predominate in it, and are the most intelligent in it when called upon for service, I would like to know the explanation of this case, and what steps the minister has taken in this regard.
I beg to move the adjournment of the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that it would have been sufficient for my hon. friend simply to have made his inquiry without trying to weave into the discussion a number of things which have no bearing upon it. I do not intend to follow him, but I will give to the House tlie best explanation I have of the matter to which reference has been made in the papers. I may say that this morning my hon. friend called me up by telephone, not so very early, and asked me if I had read this article or comment in the ' Citizen.' Ai that time I had not read it, but later on I did, and at about the same time I received a telegram, which was at my office when I arrived there this morning. It was in the following language :
London, Ontario, June 12, 1905. Sir Frederick Borden,
*Minister of Militia, Ottawa.
Reported several men from barracks ordered to Niagara to-day. Tuesday is election day Mr. SAM. HUGHES.
here and I should like it arranged to permit the men to vote before they leave.
(Sgd.) C. S. HYMAN.
So evidently, although the ' Citizen ' seems to have absolute knowledge, and my hon. friend also, as to the politics of these noncommissioned officers and men, my friend (Mr. Hyman) seems to have a different view with regard to them.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext: There is a state of uncertainty.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext:
So I think, so far as politics are concerned, we may consider the matter square, and not of very much consequence in the approaching election Now, as to the military side, 1 shall read a memorandum which I have received. I may say that when I reached my office 1 at ouce asked for an explanation of the item in the ' Citizen.' I had heard nothing ot the case, knew nothing of it absolutely, and this is the explanation which has been sent to me by the Adjutant General :
The non-commissioned officers detailed to proceed from London to Niagara, were detailed for the following reasons :	.
1.	The number of infantry to be trained at Niagara being largely in excess of that being trained at London necessitated the employment of a larger number of non-commissioned officers of the permanent infantry for instructional duties than could be furnished from No. 2 regimental depot (Toronto).
2.	No. 2 Company, Royal Canadian Regiment (Toronto), is under orders to proceed^ to Halifax and may have to move at any time on a few hours' notice.
Under these circumstances, it became a matter of urgent necessity to make sure that, as far as'possible, a sufficient supply of experienced non-commissioned officers would be avau-!*hio fnr dnt.v at eamo at Niagara.
This is the regimental order, a copy of which was sent to me by the Adjutant General :
Extract from Regimental Order No. 330.
8th June, 1905.
Detailed for duty :
The undermentioned non-commissioned officers will proceed from No. 1 Regimental Depot, Royal Canadian Regiment, to Niagara camp for instructional and other duties in connection with the camp there. They will report to the C. S. O. at Niagara on the 12th instant on arrival. These non-commissioned officers will, at the conclusion of the camp, be taken on the strength at No. 2 Regimental Depot until further orders.
No. 3407 Q.M.S.I. E. H. Price.
No. 3536 Q.M.S.I. A. B. Blake-Forster.
No. 3005 Col. Sergt. D. Cranston.
No. 3095 Sergt. M. O'Connell.
No. 3776 Sergt. W. Beales.
No. 3040 Sergt. G. Evans.
Q.M.S.I.'s Blake-Forster and Price -will report to the Adjutant of the Canadian School of Musketry on the morning of the 3rd proximo.
On receiving the telephone message from my hon. friend (Mr. Sam. Hughes) and the telegram, which I have read, from (Mr. JUXE 12, 1905
Hyman), I made inquiry as to the whereabouts of the men, and I found they were some two or three hours on their way to Niagara. Consequently I sent this telegram to Mr. Hyman :
Ottawa, 12th June, 1905.

speechtext:
Hyman,
London, Ontario.
Am informed by the Adjutant General the order cannot be cancelled as the detachment has already started for Niagara, and services urgently required there.
(Sgd.) F. tV. BORDEN.
Now, one word more in conclusion as to the men going on Monday instead of tomorrow :	I know enough about the camps
to know that it is always important to have a number of non-commissioned officers on hand at the beginning of the camp to assist in laying out the ground and to carry out the instructions of officers in preparing for the large number of troops who are to come in. This is all the explanation I have to give, and it seems to me it ought to be accepted as ample.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext: The lion. Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) has referred to a telegram sent to him by lion. Mr. Hyman, also his answer to it. I do not understand from his remarks that he intends to give these men opportunity to vote tomorrow in London. Now, I wish to point out that this is a matter which has been talked of pretty freely in London, and has found its way into the public press in that c-ity. I may say to the Minister of Militia also that the politicians in London are regarded as a ' slick gang,' to use an expression that they themselves would use. This little by-play has been very well arranged, and I have no doubt it has worked out just as the hon. gentleman has stated. And any one who knows the facts knows perfectly well that if these men had been left in the city to vote they would not have voted for Mr. Hyman. So, it is arranged that they are not to be there, and this little by-play is gone through for the benefit of the public. There is the whole ease in a nutshell. I am surprised that the Minister of Militia and Defence makes no effort to arrange that these men are to have an opportunity to vote.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext:
It would be interesting to know the precise time when this matter came to the attention of Mr. Hyman. It has been referred to in the press of London this morning, and it seems a little peculiar that no telegram was received from that gentleman until reference had -been made to the matter in the public press both of London and of Ottawa. It seems a little peculiar, to say the least of it, that Mr. Hyman should know nothing of it except from the press. We have had a somewhat higher opinion of his knowledge of what was going on at the present moment in the city of
London than to suppose that he needed information on such points as this from the public press. I heard of it before to-day myself. On Saturday night I heard the rumour; that these men were to be sent away, and I got a telegram on the subject very early this morning from certain Conservatives in London. It is rather remarkable, certainly and, whether remarkable or not, it is quite timely, that Mr. Hyman should telegraph when he did.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext: After the men had gone.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext:
When they were two or three hours on their journey, Mr. Hyman, because considerable indignation is aroused in London, sends a telegram. And this telegram, the minister produces with a certain smile and a certain look out of the corner of his eye. And he turns to my hon. friend (Mr. Sam. Hughes) and says :	' It
does not look as if there was much politics in it ; besides the men are two or three hours on their way and it is impossible that they can be recalled.' It looks like a very well devised piece of play, a very pretty little game. But I do not think that any one's understanding of the real situation will be altered by the fact that Mr. Hyman sent a telegram at nine or ten o'clock this morning after the men had gone and when he. no doubt, thoroughly understood, that the decision of the Department of Militia would be that they should not be recalled. The telegram I received spoke not of six men. but of seven men who are supposed to be Conservatives, and who only on Saturday were ordered to start from London to Niagara this morning.
I think it would take a little more than Mr. Hyman's telegram or any such explanation as we have had this afternoon to convince any man in this House, or in this country, that there was not some little design in all this. It was very easy to bring in a pretty little report from some gentleman of the Department of Militia pointing out the necessity-the ' urgent necessity,' for it is stated that this is not only a ' necessity,' but that it is * urgent '-that these men should start on Monday, the day before election. I think we shall all have our opinion on the subject. tVbile their instruction may be necessary for camp on Wednesday, there is not a word in the communication read by the minister which, to my mind, leads to the conclusion that the men are wanted there before W ed-nesday. The minister speaks of the necessity of having a number of men on hand to make preparation for the camp. But. surely, with the hundreds of men to be assembled there to-morrow every preparation for the instruction which is only to begin on Wednesday could have been made without bringing these seven men from London. We are not to believe the reverse of that even from the minister's statement. Well, it seems tome this is a pretty small piece of business I to come down to after all-on the eve of an

election in London, a by-election, the verdict in which, according to the statements of members of the administration will be significant, it is a pretty small piece of business to send seven men from London to Niagara under circumstances that do not leave much room for doubt in the mind of any man who examines the evidence as to the real motive which led to the making of the order at that particular juncture.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext: I think a little inquiry in regard to dates may be of interest here. The general order has no date, but it must have been issued some time before the regimental order. The general order is the order changing the usual practice and providing for the sending of noncommissioned officers from London instead of from Toronto. An apparently good reason is given for that by the Minister of Militia-the fact that the permanent corps at Toronto has been ordered to Halifax-

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext: It is not going for some time.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext:
I agree, with my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, that this would be a very small piece of business-a conspiracy entered into in order to deprive men who have the right to vote under our law, from casting their ballots. But my hon. friend the leader of the opposition will agree with me that it would be a still smaller piece of business to charge the Department of Militia with having been guilty of an act of this kind, unless there is absolute proof. There is no evidence whatever that the thing which is complained of has been done designedly, and 1 can understand that it has been done in the ordinary routine of the Militia Department. A camp is opening to-morrow at Niagara, and as I understand from the statement made by the Minister of Militia, corroborated by the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Tisdale), these men, non-commissioned officers, have to be there to discharge their duty on the opening of the camp; and therefore, if there had been no election, they would have had to go just the same; and probably the militia officers who made this order did not think, it did not occur to them at the time, that there was an election in London on Tuesday. They had in mind only their military duties, and they had to provide a certain number of non-commissioned officers to open the camp, to be there, not on the day the camp opens, but on the day before, to prepare the ground and to do whatever was necessary to be done. If that be so, can it be charged that the Department of Militia acted in connivance with the Liberal candidate in order to help his election? I would be sorry for my part to believe it, I do not believe it, and I will not believe it. at all events, until some fact is brought forward to justify the charge. Now it has been said there was a little by-play between Mr. Hyman and the militia officers, because Mr. Hyman only sent his telegram to-day. Well, as I understand it. nobody knew of this order until Saturday, on Saturday there was a rumpus and excitement, and Mr. Hyman, who is a very busy man to-day. might have been there this morning or yesterday, and somebody on the Conservative side came to Air. Hyman and told him this order would deprive a certain number of his opponents from voting, and Mr. Hyman, with that chivalry which characterizes him, at once telegraphed to the Minister of Militia.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext:
At the last general election which was held on the 3rd of November, and on the second day before it, the pay of these men was raised 25 cents a day. What was the object?
Sir WILih'KID LAURIER. That addition to the pay was decided on in the previous session of parliament, and that order was only giving effect to it, there was nothing new in that. My hon. friend knows as well as I do that this increase in pay had been decided on by Act of this parliament at the previous session. Therefore, I think that there is no ground for suspicion of any collusion. I have only this to say, that I hope we shall cease to cast aspersions upon one another's good faith unless there is clear evidence.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext: I do not wish to animadvert in any way upon hon. gentlemen opposite, but it does seem to me that there is a disposition on the part or some of them always to find fault and to attribute improper motives. Now I take no exception to what my hon. friend from South Norfolk has said. I think his statement on the whole is very fair, and I feel disposed, if it can be done without injury to the public service, to act upon the suggestion he has made. I wish to say, however, that I knew absolutely nothing about the general order, or about the reasons for it. until my attention was called to this matter this morning. There was no collusion or connivance. I do not believe there has been anything improper intended in any quarter. There is something like a hundred men in the depot at London, and this is a proposal to move six selected men. I presume the best men for the purpose, from London, men who are wanted for instructional purposes.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext: Is there not a camp held at London?

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext: In telegraphic communications-and several have been passed to me on this subject-emphasis is laid upon the circumstance that there is a camp being held in London at which these men are really wanted. I do not know how correct that may be, but it is a circumstance which lends colour and force to the belief, on the part of the Conservatives of London at least, that the men have been ordered to Niagara for reasons connected with the election contest in London.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext: I can understand that, but as I have stated already, the whole of the company stationed at Toronto from which the non-commissioned officers would naturally be drawn to take part in the Niagara camp, has been ordered out in readiness to go to Halifax at any moment, and is liable to be ordered to Halifax at any moment.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext: No actual date is set?

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext: No, but ready and liable to be moved at any moment, and that is the reason, and I believe it is the only reason. But in view of the fact that such improper motives are attributed to the department, and with a desire to prevent the evil effect attendant upon all. these accusations which are hurled against the management of the militia, and which are calculated to have a prejudicial effect upon the militia, I am prepared to accede to the suggestion made by my hon. friend from South Norfolk, and I will send at once to the Adjutant General to come here and see whether an arrangement can be made, without the public interest suffering too much, by which these men can be returned to London and sent back on Wednesday or on Tuesday night. If my hon. friends opposite will accept that statement, perhaps the incident may be closed-and I will inform the House later on as to the result of my inquiry.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext: I think the minister has met the case very fairly indeed, and I hope lie will not insist on the conditional words at the end of his promise-' if it can be done without the public interest suffering too much.'

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext: I will put a broad interpretation upon that.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext: I think we are all common-sense people. Now that Rojestven-sky's fleet is under the sea and various other matters have happened, I do not think that great peril will ensue to this country if these men are allowed to go back and vote on whichever side they please. The right hon. gentleman stated that we had nothing but circumstantial evidence on which to base our suspicions ; and then he made an argument on the other side which stood equally on circumstantial evidence. I think the gist of the whole thing lies here : That rightly or wrongly, a large number of people in this country will think that a game is being played with the militia, and I do not think we can afford to have that done. I am quite willing to attribute the most chivalrous feelings to all politicians and all public men, and especially to the present members of the ministry, and prospective members of the ministry ; at the same time, I am not disposed to think that the candidate running in London in the ministerial interest is not a very sharp and wide-awake politician, and I think that at the present time in London both candidates will believe that eight votes are worth making a struggle for-

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext:
Only six.
Mr. FOSTER,-or six are worth making a struggle for and it is hard work for me to believe that Mr. Hyman was so diligent

in attending to his c-hurch duties yesterday, or resting on the Sabbath day, as not to know that from Saturday to Monday morning at nine o'clock something was going on in this direction.	I think
the hon. minister is well advised and that be meets this side of the House fairly when he virtually says that these men shall go back and be allowed to vote.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.
speechtext: I am very much pleased that the hon. minister lias taken the stand he has in this connection. Now, however, that the matter is up I will just repeat the case. I make the statement without fear of contradiction that that telegram from Mr. Hyman was arranged for.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF LONDON MILITIAMEN AT NIAGARA.

Order.

speechtext: I make the statement that the telegram was arranged for. It is a piece of by-play, as my hon. friend has stated. These men were sent away because they were Conservatives. I would ask the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence to follow this matter up. speechtext: Oh.

speechtext:
If that little babbling Sbarretti message boy will kindly keep ciuiet we will get on very nicely. AVe want these men to have their votes in London. They are entitled to their votes and if we can secure them for them they are going to have them. If they vote for Air. Hyman all right ; they are exercising their franchise. If they vote for Air. Gray it is all the same ; they are exercising their franchise and no one has a right to question that. I venture to say that the grounds have already been located and laid out. The hon. minister's argument was that these men were wanted to lay out the camp. I will venture to say that every regiment has sent its men in advance to prepare for the camp. These instructors are not the men who will be employed to Mr. FOSTER.
lay out the camp. The men who lay out the grounds are, not the men who go from London but from Toronto. The grounds are laid out by another- set of men altogether.

Not at all. It is a few hours' job at best. Then it is said that they are there to receive the regiments -when they come in. There is a little too much at times of paternally looking after the regiments when they come into camp. I have had a considerable amount of experience in regard to that matter and I have never yet seen the necessity for any non-commissioned officers stepping in to receive a regiment when it comes in. These men are not attached to apron strings, they can look after themselves and not one of these non-commissioned officers will be necessary in the camp at all. I was going to ask the hon. minister to give these men permission to go back, but I want the hon. minister to follow this matter up still further. In connection with Colonel Gregory we have an instance of an officer commanding a district interfering in the most objectionable way-and we will hear more of that, I hope, before the end of the session

to get rid of Colonel Gregory. Some officer has furnished the names here. Some officer has been asked to send these men to Niagara. I want the hon. minister to be good enough to bring down all the correspondence in connection with it. AA'ho demanded the sending of these men to Niagara camp ? AY ho selected the men who were to go ? AA'as it by chance that six or seven Conservatives were selected ? Possibly there were none others to go. If that is the explanation, all right. I would like to ask the hon. minister how many lion-commissioned officers are there amongst the hundred men at the London camp. . I trow he will find that there are very few left in the London camp and he must know that these men are wanted in London for one week more. Do I understand the hon. minister that he is going to furnish these men with transport and sustenance in going from Niagara to London and from London back to Niagara ? I trust the hon. minister will not only give them permission to go but that he" will furnish them with transport and sustenance at the cost of the Dominion of Canada.

Bill (No. 169) to amend the Act respecting the Royal Military College-Sir Frederick Borden-read a second time and House wrent into committee thereon.
On section 1,
You do not seem to have fixed a maximum expenditure here as you promised.

At the conclusion of the debate on the resolution, 1 understood my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) to state that there was no particular point in filling in the amount, and I rather thought that idea was accepted.
I did not say that, but 1 qualified it by saying it was my individual view. The resolution is wide enough to allow an amount to be fixed.

Very well.
I move to amend the section by inserting after the word ' council,' the words ' but shall not exceed in all $30,000.'
This clause limits the salary of the head of the Royal Military College to $3,200 per annum ; I suppose there are allowances also ?
Yes, there is a house and a good many other things besides. The salary was increased to that amount in 1893.

My opinion is that the educationists of this country both civil and military are not paid as they should be. I would be very much pleased if the resolution should read that the salary should be * not less than $3,200,' instead of, ' not more than $3,200.'
Including the allowances the salary provided is a very comfortable one and it has enabled us to get a veiy efficient officer.

I would move that the clause should read that : the salary of the commandant shall not exceed $3,200 a year ; the salaries of the staff adjutants and professors, instructors and assistant instructors and staff, shall uot exceed a total sum of $30,000 annually.

On tlie order being called :
Second reading of Bill (No. 170) to amend the Militia Act.-Sir Frederick Borden.

Might I make a suggestion to tile minister before we proceed to consider this order. It will be prettv difficult to go into a full discussion of this Bill unless we have the correspondence that has passed between the imperial government and the Canadian government with reference to taking over the defences at Halifax and Esquimau, so that we may know what is the position of each government in connection therewith. As a layman I say this is important, because it seems to'bring out pretty sharply the line of demarcation between a standing army and the militia of the country ; at least it is showing a deeidediy strong tendency towards the establishment of a regular army-not very large, 5,000 men-but still it brings up the whole question as to how far this country should go in that direction and whether it is possible for us to provide sufficient money to have a respectable standing army and at the same time do full justice to our militia, the real arm of our defence. The cost of regulars as high and although you may have only 3,000 in addition to those you now have, the sum total that will be required for the maintenance of these
3,000	men will be pretty large. Then in the second place, if we take over these fortifications, if there is no other way but that we shall do that, we incur an unknown expense of large proportions at the least, which may become very large under circumstances that may occur, it is well for us, I think, to talk over this matter before we have committed ourselves, before the second reading of this Bill, and see whether or not there is not another and a better way by which the same object can be brought about of retaining these defences and retaining them in the only way in which they would be useful, that is as absolutely modern and up-to-date fortifications and defences, therefore, it seems to me to be necessary to have that correspondence, and be able to look over it before the House should be called upon to pledge itself to a policy which is proposed by the government of taking these stations over and of laying the foundation of a regular army. Another point on which I would like Information is as to the cost. I find that in this and that newspaper calculations are made as to what the cost will be. These estimates may be near the mark and they may be a long way from it; we have to rely upon what our department gives us, and I would like the minister to have his council, those with whom he consults, make very careful estimates as to what will be the added cost. As I understand it. we

have now about 1.200 men belonging to the permanent force.
S*ir FREDERICK BORDEN. Something over that.

And provision has been wade to increase that to about 2,000. We would like to know what that extra cost will be when our standing force is brought up to 2,000. Then we would like to know, with as much certainty as we can possibly have, what the extra 3,000 men will cost as distributed in the two stations, with all that is necessary to keep them efficient, taking into consideration the difficulty-and I think my hon. friend will find a difficulty-of getting eligible Canadians to go into the permanent force at the very low rate of wages for which the British government lias been able to keep regulars in its service. It is becoming more difficult for them to do this, as I find by the conferences and discussions that are taking place in the British parliament. And in the United States they find it difficult to recruit men unless they pay them well. I do not imagine that in the future this item will keep at the figure at which it is to-day in the regular British service. I think we will have to face the idea of having that largely increased instead of remaining at the present rate. Well, then, if you are going to put 3,000 men at Halifax and at Esquimalt, and undertake the c-are of these fortresses, we do not want to do that simply to have two toys and somewhat expensive toys, one at each end of our country ; we want to have a station at the Pacific 'and another at the Atlantic which will be absolutely serviceable and up-to-date hi every respect. We do not know the conditions upon which we are entering into this. We have to keep up the fortifications, and, that being so, we must face the cost of keeping them up-to-date and of going as fai as modern improvements make it necessary to go, discarding one set of arms and taking another and more expensive set as circumstances require. That, of course, is a matter upon which we cannot get estimates, but we can get estimates as to what it will cost for the .men themselves and their keep, and what it will cost per year for keeping up the fortifications to the point of proficiency at which, I suppose, we aim to keep them, or we would not undertake them at all. Then, when we get that as a foundation,. we will be able to discuss the general principle as to whether Canada should not be dependent almost entirely upon its militia rather than attempt even a small standing army, and so to keep down the permanent force to what is absolutely necessary for instructional and educational purposes, and to go no further than that. I do not know what military men think of the circumstances which have developed in the South African war and the present war, but it does seem to me that things have taken on a very different aspect. I think that num-

bers and shooting power are what should be aimed at by a country that wishes to defend itself, and therefore by Canada, even though we do not now, and I hope never shall, think of undertaking an aggressive war, but still we have a country so vast and so rich that we must make its defence fairly well assured, and it seems to me that the lessons of the wars that have just passed go to show that what you want is men who can handle arms and shoot well and have numbers of such easily available. It is apparently the large numbers that avail, together with proficiency, and it is not so difficult a matter to knock an army into fighting shape now as it seemed to be under the old regime, when it was thought that no one was fit for warfare except the regulars who had been almost born and bred to it. These are the considerations which led me to ask the minister to allow this item to stand until we have obtained the information for which I have asked. Then, too, the House is very thin, and this is a very interesting question to all military men. We shall not lose by having as full a House as possible to discuss the question when once it comes up. So far as I am concerned, I feel very much disinclined to vote money for anything that appears like a standing army, vve must have instructors and we must have a nucleus. So far as that goes, we ought to have it efficient, no matter what the cost. If we go beyond that and have even a small force of regulars, very costly and without any power of multiplying itself in case of actual war, I think we would be adopting a policy that would not redound much to the benefit of the country. Of course, I speak with diffidence in this, because I am not a military man.

I must congratulate my hon. friend upon the progress which he is making, and I welcome him very much into the discussion of these important matters. I wish that more hon. gentlemen would take the trouble to read and think about them. But I will say while I entirely acquiesce in his desire to postpone the discussion of this Bill, I think it might he proper that I should say one or two words to 'set his mind at rest as to one or two points in which I think he misunderstands the position.
I would not take it amiss, in fact I should prefer to have the minister give as much information as possible, because it will help us in the consideration of this measure.

What I wish to say at the outset is that there is no intention whatever to take any steps towards the establishment of a standing army; there is no intention to depart in the slightest degree from the policy which was adopted by this country shortly after confederation, , and which has been followed ever since, of
providing depots of a permanent force for the purpose chiefly of educating the active militia of the country, upon which we would almost exclusively rely for defence.
I am afraid that my hon. friend, in his desire to acquire information has been looking in the wrong quarter." l myself have seen recently one or two articles which absolutely misrepresent the situation. I do not mean to say that this misrepresentation was intentional, so perhaps it would be more accurate to say that the writers misapprehended the situation. As I have said, there is not the slightest scintilla of evidence to prove the allegation- nor is there the slightest particle of truth in that allegation-that we are going to establish, or have any idea of establishing, a standing army. So far as it goes, the fact that we are going to take over the garrisons at Halifax and Esquimalt and substitute for the units of the imperial army of these two places Canadinu soldiers. might be said to be some excuse for the statement that we are establishing a standing army; but only so far. And, in that connection, let me say that it is the intention of the Militia Council and of the government to utilize these two depots just, as all the other depots are used for instructional purposes of the militia- that at Halifax for the militia of the maritime provinces, and that at Esquimalt for the militia of British Columbia. Now, whether we should or should not take over these two garrisons, whether we should or should not relieve the British taxpayer of the expense of their maintenance, Is a question of policy, a question on which we may reasonably differ. But the government has made the offer, the offer has been accepted ; and so far as the government is concerned, it is committed to carry that offer into execution. I was under the impression-I am still under the impression-that the House, including my hon. friend (Mr. Foster), and the country generally, would approve of this additional step in the direction of assuming responsibility for the defence of Canada upon Canadian soil.
Now, as to the policy outside of these two garrisons, I said a moment ago that we are continuing a system adopted shortly after confederation, the policy of maintaining a permanent militia force-not a standing army, but a number of officers, noncommissioned officers and men, permanently employed, chiefly for instructional purposes but incidentally for the purpose of guarding and taking charge of fortifications at different points. At the outset confederation was limited to four provinces, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. A little later Prince Edward Island came in. Depots for the permanent force were established at Toronto, London, Kingston, Quebec, St. John's (Quebec) and Fredericton, for the purposes I have just

indicated. They are maintained still, at very much the strength at which they were maintained in the early days of coil-federation and for the purposes for which they were established. But the country has grown. There is a Northwest. And when the province of Manitoba, became a province a depot was established there.
Would the minister allow me at this point to ask him how about the Strathcona Horse, of Calgary ?

I was coming to that. The province of Manitoba was established, and the idea of an instructional force was carried out there, a depot being established at Winnipeg. In the Northwest Territories, it was not thought wise to establish the militia. Instead of the militia, a force of police, known now as the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, was established in the unorganized section of the country. In the province of British Columbia there was a British garrison. Now, we are about to establish two new provinces. The work of defending and maintaining civil order in these provinces will devolve upon the militia force. It is proposed to continue in these provinces the work begun in the east, of establishing instructional depots, and the depot referred to by my hon. friend (Mr. Sam. Hughes), that of the Strathcona Horse will be one.

I do not wish to interrupt the hon. minister, but I would be glad if he would explain the reason why we should establish depots in the new provinces when we have stiH the Northwest Mounted Police ? I have not heard that that body is to be abolished. The mere fact of their being autonomous provinces will not change the condition in that respect.

It will, to a very large extent. In addition to what 1 have said in the early years the question of defending the Northwest was a question that was not seriously considered; the practical question was largely the defence of the eastern and more populous provinces. These Territories are becoming populous and new provinces are being created. The scheme of defence which was begun in the east, is being gradually carried through the west and through British Columbia to the Pacific coast. And the idea is-and I believe it is a sound one-to carry out this policy of organizing a chain of depots of the permanent force from the Atlantic through the older provinces, through the Northwest, through British Columbia, to the Pacific coast-depots which will be in touch with each other and which will form the nucleus of an effective militia which will afford instruction to all the militia.
Now, 1 have explained very briefly, and perhaps imperfectly, the scheme which we Sir F. W. BORDEN.
have in mind-which is no new scheme but is simpiy the amplification of the policy established long ago. Now, to come to the Bill. Last year the policy was to increase the permanent force from 1,000 to 2,000 men. In the early years of confederation, 1,000 men were sufficient for the few depots in the east. But the country has grown and we thought 2,000 would be necessary. Now, it is proposed to add a depot at Montreal, to increase the force by this additional depot and by one in the Northwest. I am now advised that it is desirable to increase the number in the Northwest, not immediately. but eventually, in order to carry out this scheme. And we are now taking over the garrisons at Halifax on the one hand and Esquimalt on the other.
Is there at present a depot in Montreal?
No.
And you propose to put one there? You have one at St. Johns and one at Quebec-npretty close quarters.
The depot at St. Johns is on the frontier and is of special importance for that reason-just as tiie one at Fredericton which would not have been placed there but for a similar consideration.
I understand the depot at St. Johns is for cavalry. It would not be quite the same thing as the other.

No. Now, I would have said, if I had been anxious to proceed with the Bill to-day, which I am not specially, that we could very well have taken up this Bill and taken the power-because taking of this power is all the Bill amounts to-to increase the permanent force to 5,000 men. Of these, 2,000 or thereabouts will be necessary for the garrisons at Halifax and Esquimalt, and something less than 2,000 for all the other depots, leaving a margin of perhaps. 1,000 to be tilled in later on. I explained the other day that while this number would not be required all at once, there was no doubt that, rvith the growth of the country, in the near future 5,000 would probably be required, and that I thought we might as well take authority now to raise that number instead of coming back at some later date. But I believe 5,000 is the full number that will be required by Canada for many years.
What is the number now ?
About 1,250. not including those who have been sent to Halifax. But that is not enough, the normal number would be about 1,500 at present, if Montreal were included.
That is, you are increasing the number to 3,800, as a matter of fact ?
Yes. Now with regard to Halifax and Esquimau, I will not speak at present.
Is that correspondence nearly ready ?

I am waiting for the final touches, the final answer, from the war office, certain details which 1 hope to have at any moment. I do not think I can add any more except to say that the information which my hon. friend has asked for is being prepared. As a matter of fact, when the debate comes on which has been promised upon one of the large items of the militia vote, I expect to lay on the table of the House a memorandum, and to put it in the hands of every member, which will show what the expenditure is, and what is in volved in all this scheme.
Would the hon. gentleman say what will be the number of men in garrison at Halifax when it is full ?

The present number is about 1,S00 to 2,000 of British troops. I am told by General Lake that he expects to be able to do the same work with from 1,200 to 1,400.
Mr. BERGERON As a matter of fact, is it not true that it is very .hard for my hon. friend to fill up that establishment ?

No. I am glad that question has been asked, because it gives me an opportunity of reading to the House a letter which 1 received just as 1 came in, from the Adjutant General. It is as follows :
Dear Sir Frederick.-I desire to call attention to an article in this morning's ' Citizen ' on military matters. ' In this article it is stated that we caninot get sufficient recruits because the pay is too small. This is not the case. The Canadian soldier is the highest paid soldier in the world to-day, receiving as he does $15 per month during the first year of service, with a material increase in the second and third years. As paragraphs of this nature are calculated to hinder recruiting for Halifax and Esquimau, I trust you will take steps to have this statement^in regard to insufficiency of pay publicly contradicted.
As a matter of fact we have had no difficulty whatever in getting all the recruits we wanted. The statement is absolutely without foundation, and calculated, as the Adjutant General says, to cause unnecessary trouble and worry.
ilr. SAM. HUGHES. I understood from the statement that the minister had difficulty in getting recruits, that there were only 900 now, when the statute calls for 1,200.

I know my hon. friend relies upon reports In the papers, and will not accept my official statement. I am sorry, but I cannot help it. I can assure my hon. friend, if he ever gets into office, he will find that these mischievous reports,
and intentionally mischievous reports, are very injurious, and will be very injurious to his administration.
Is the Kingston battery establishment filled up now ?
I do not wish to be cross examined ; but I have stated bere, I am told, tliat the force is practically full.
That letter does not say the force is full, it merely defends the pay, and shows that the reason the men are not enlisting Is because of insufficiency.

Then I am not able to understand the letter of the Adjutant General. But as I do understand it, it means that we have no difficulty in getting all the permanent troops we require. Now one more word as to this standing army question, as to the allegations that are made, without the slightest foundation, that in order to be able to increase tbe number of depots and to take over the garrisons of Halifax and Esquimalt, we are cutting down tbe militia, we are robbing Peter to pay Paul. There is not the slightest foundation of truth in that statement at all. W c are taking over xiaiiiax and Lsquimait to relieve the British taxpayer, and not to cut down the militia. There is no intention to reduce the expenditure upon the active militia because of taking over these two forts. It would be what might be called an Indian gift to do anything like that. While we would be relieving the British taxpayer, we would not be strengthening the British Crown and its power in this country if we were to cut down the active militia, while using the money saved In that way to pay for the garrisons at Halifax and Esquimalt. No such contemptible idea has entered into my mind, or the mind of any member of this government. I can not understand the motive which anybody would have-I am not addressing anybody in this House, but outside of the House-who may pretend to be a military critic, in putting forward a statement of that kind. On the 31st of May last the correspondent of the London 'Times' in this city cabled to England a state; ment, which was published in tlie ' Times,' to the effect that in order to be able to take over the Halifax and Esquimalt garrisons every regiment in Canada had been denuded of one of its companies, and that there had been a general reduction all along the line of the active militia. The statement is absolutely without foundation. If the man who sent that cablegram did not know any better, it was his duty to this country-I believe he is not a native of this country- it was his duty to this country, and his duty to the newspaper to whom he was sending his correspondence, and his duty to this government to come to me or to the department and get proper information before he sent a mischievous cablegram of that kind.

Now as a matter of fact, the active militia is being increased continuously every year ; every year since I came into office there has been an increase. This year there will be
6,000	or 7,000 more men of the active militia trained in camps than ever before in this country, at any rate since 1870 at the time of the Fenian trouble. There is no truth, I repeat it again, in the statement that we have adopted the policy of establishing a standing army here ; and there is no truth in the statement that we are taking over and paying for garrisons at Halifax and Esqui-malt at the expense of the active militia, and such a statement is as unfair as it is untrue.

Accepting the hon. gentleman's explanation that he is not doing this to the detriment of the militia of Canada, as a matter of fact, what will be the cost to the taxpayers of Canada of these two garrisons at Esquimalt and Halifax ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think that if a discussion is going on there should be a motion for the second reading of the Bill, or a motion to adjourn.
I thought the second reading had been moved. I move that the Bill be now read the second time.

The hon. minister stated that the establishment was completed. I hold in my hand the minister's own report and I find that the establishment of the permanent corps for 1904 was 1,24a. The strength on December 31, 1904, was 959.

I am sure my hon. friend does not wish to draw inferences from that report which are not correct. That may have been the number then, but I stated that at the present time the strength of the corps is nearly 1,300.

This is the latest and only information that the public has in Sir F. W. BORDEN.
the matter. The hon. minister is a little out of place in censuring any one for taking the official figures of the strength of the corps which are given as 959. To know the strength we turn to the report of the minister. The minister must not think that the public can learn these things by intuition.
But if the public prefers to read the reports of persons who are unable to give the information rather than to read the statement I have made in the House I cannot help it.

I would like to add a word to what the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has said on two lines. The first and most particular information we want is as to the expenditures past and present. I will try to give a little summary so that the minister may have the information prepared as far as he can obtain it : (1) the number of men kept by the British government in these two garrisons ; (2) the number. of men the department propose to ask the House to confirm and the number they propose to substitute. Iu all possibility it may be much less or much more.
As definite as possible. .
I would like a positive statement of the estimate of the number that would he required.
As definite as possible.

As definite as possible, but in figures ; (3) the estimated expenditures of the war office, if they have it, on these men and all other expenses, if they have it, connected with the maintenance of the establishment and the pay, or in any way connected with the garrison ; (4) the estimated expenditures of the cost of the number of men who are to be substituted and their incidentals ; (5) the estimated expenditures of the fortifications themselves for the year. I think we are entitled to this Information and that is all I wish.
I wil] give a 'A I can.
Not only what you can, because I will explain why I want it as fully as possible. It may he a'little trouble but those who with yourself are responsible should figure out what you propose.
We are doing that.
In other words there may be anticipated a very large expenditure. It will all depend on how these fortifications are manned and armed at the present time.

My hon. friend will see, if I may interrupt him, that this is something that it is impossible to

give because I do not know and I could not find out, I fancy, without the greatest difficulty, what the nature of the defences of Halifax are. It is known to be one of the most powerful fortresses in the world, but very few people know the number of guns, and it is not desirable that they should know.

I do not want to know the number of guns. Without the expenditures I am foreshowing it is impossible to determine this important question. This information would have very great weight upon the question of principle which is involved. The hon. minister has assumed that the members on both sides of the House are in favour of this principle, but when the hon. gentleman assumes to believe that the House and the country are in favour of the principle of the government taking over these fortifications and supplying these garrisons I am not prepared at all to agree with him. I am not at ail prepared to agree to the principle in my present state of mind and with the information I have. At all events, I know that there are a great many other people in this country, some of them military who have mentioned it to myself, and others who are not military, who are not in favour of the proposition laid down in this House and in the country that the government should take over these garrisons and these fortifications. It depends on circumstances, so far as I am concerned, before I make up my mind. This country and this House are" in favour of Canada doing more towards defence, but I am not at all satisfied for myself, and I do not believe the country is, until we know more about it, that I should vote in favour of this proposition. I merely say this now because the hon. gentleman assumes that the House is in favour of the proposition and if later on some hon. gentlemen object to it, I do not wish it to appear as if we have assented to it at one time and objected to it afterwards. The care of fortifications is an entirely new work for the Dominion of Canada. We have no experience in regard to it. The hon. minister has made a very grave admission, a most serious admission and possibly it might be well for me to follow that up a little and call his attention to it. He frankly admits he has no idea of the nature of the magnificent defences, preparations and armaments at Halifax. That is what I complain of and what the people object to, if I do not disagree with him. Wfe have no idea of what it is going to cost or of our capabilities of manning and properly handling these defences. This is practically a matter in which we have no experience because as a rule the militia have nothing to do with fortifications and are not capable of manning them because they are not trained to such work. In these modern days it is believed that forts are no good. It is accepted as a gen-231
eral proposition and it is only in exceptional cases where enormous expenditures are being made and where they are always ready to change the equipment as .the evolution of the day indicates the necessity of new styles of arms that a fortress proves effective. It is most important that parliament should know what the government is committing this country to, and that we are capable of maintaining and providing for these defences if the empire is going to rely upon us. The minister has practically admitted to-day that he knows nothing about it.
No, I said it was impossible for me to tell what type of guns would be used, but I do not think there is much difficulty in getting the expenditure, not perhaps to a dollar but practically.

Do you know what it L eans to undertake the defence of two fortifications that ought be second to none in the world so that the fleet of Great Britain, may be safe under the guns of these forts. That is a thing that requires serious consideration. I want to know what the cost will be for five or ten years to come. I will go as far as any one eise to endorse any reasonable expenditure for the defence of Canada and the empire, but I want to be sure that we know what we are undertaking and I want to be certain also that our maintainance of these fortifications so vital to the empire, will be thorough. I would have a great deal of hesitation about committing myself to this proposition without further information. I agree to a certain extent with my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) in regard to a standing army. I suppose there is a distinction between a permanent force and a standing army; the difference may be in the name but a rose by any other name would smell as sweet. So far, our permanent force has been confined to schools of instruction, to aiding the civil power so that the volunteers may not be involved, and as forming a nucleus which we may rely ou in case we want- to call out a large military force. But now you are going to put the permanent force into fortifications, and they must be instructed in the most modern military tactics.
Is not that desirable for Canada ?
Desirable for Canada if we are to defend these outposts of the empire.
We will never acquire that military information unless we begin.

Don't begin too fast, and don't begin unnecessarily, and don't forget that you are now undertaking not only to defend Canadian interests but imperial interests as well. It is one thing to provide



for the defences of Canada alone, and it is another thing to undertake the defence of the empire.
Canada is a part of the empire.

If these fortifications were only for the defence of Canada it would be an entirely different thing. I do not want to oppose this proposition if I possibly can avoid it, but I certainly must know what we are doing before I support it. Speaking as a Canadian I would be proud to make an expenditure for the joint defence of the empire and of Canada, but it goes past pride and becomes conceit when any one thinks that the defence of Canada is more important than the defence of the empire. I will join with the government in any reasonable expense, but I want first to know what we are about.

I wish to ask a few questions so that when we come to the discussion of this measure the minister may be prepared to give me the information. The minister told us that the militia has increased since 1896; is that in number or expense ?
Both.
What is the strength of the militia to-day ?
What is the present cost of the militia as compared with its cost in 1896.
I cannot say exactly but it is very much more than it was in 1896.
I am putting these questions so that the Minister of Militia will have the information when we come to discuss this Bill.
In 1896 the annual drill cost about $425,000 and for the present year it will cost between $700,000 and $800,000, but a large part of that is due to the increase in pay which has been almost doubled.
Whatever may have been the cause, the expenditure of the Militia Department to-day is very nearly double what it was in 1896 ?
I think so.

When this question comes up again, wall my hon. friend be in a position to say what induced the government to replace British soldiers by Canadian soldiers in the garrisons at Esquimau and [DOT]Halifax ? Was it the result of correspondence with the imperial government ?
The papers will be laid on the table as soon as completed.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER moved the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to.

House in Committee of Supply.
Grant to the imperial government to cover Canada's proportion of probable losses in connection with the operation of the Pacific cable, $125,000.
['Yes. And we hope to go into Committee of Supply taking up the estimates of the Department of Public Works.']
Are you co-owners of the cable ?
Yes.
By what arrangement?

The contract was made between the imperial government and the colonies I have mentioned in 1899 or thereabouts. There is a trust created by the four governments to manage the cables. The trust is composed of the representatives appointed by the different governments. Our representative is Lord Strath-eona and the late manager of the Montreal Bank, Mr. Lang.
Is this managed as a commercial enterprise ?
Yes ; we have borrowed the cost of construction, two million pounds. It is expected we shall repay the interest and extinguish the capital debt. The deficit is upon, the running of the cable.
What has been the income from the traffic receipts for the last five years ?

The cable has been only in operation for two years, and I have not the information the hon. gentleman asks. Our expectations have not been realized, which is largely due to the competition of the eastern companies, which have the advantage of a contract made by the South Wales government before the federation of the Australian colonies. The traffic has not been as large as we expected, but it is increasing.
I understand that New South Wales entered into an arrangement with us which it is not exactly carrying out. Has that question been settled ?
No ; we have made representations again and again to the South Wales government, but we have had no satisfaction.
Where is that cable laid?
On the Pacific coast from the shore of the island of Vancouver to Australia, passing by Fanning island, the British island to the north of Honolulu.

Are there other cables in that direction or are the others on the Atlantic?
231J

That is the only cable between Australia and the American continent on the Pacific ocean.
Mr. BEKUlKON. Then there must be another one on the other side ?
There is another one on the Atlantic.
But it has no connection with the one we are talking of.
The object was to have continuous communication over British territory from Australia to British Columbia, then across Canada and then by the Atlantic cables to Great Britain.
We have nothing to do with the cables on the Atlantic?
No, the Atlantic cable belongs to the commercial company.
We are interested in the one on the Pacific ocean.
Nothing else.
We are at the mercy of the one on the Atlantic.
The trouble is not with the Atlantic cables, but at the other end.

I do not understand that Australia has defaulted in her payment of five-tenths of the cost, but it has not given good commercial support to the cable, not such support as by the negotiations she would be bound to give. Apart from the New South Wales contract is there amongst the other Australian colonies an Indisposition to carry out their arrangements as regards commercial assistance to it? Are they giving commercial support to the proposed eastern extension?

I am not prepared to answer the hon. gentleman except as regards New South Wales. These negotiations were commenced before confederation in Australia and we made an arrangement which was completed with the Australian government and which was made with the Australian government and not with any other. But before confederation had been completed, New South Wales had made an arrangement with the eastern company and that is what we complain of. We have been protesting against that and asking the Australian government who are a party to that to in some way do away with this monopoly which they have given to the eastern company. Our representations up to the present time have been unavailing. New Zealand has supported us and has protested just as vigorously as we have because New Zealand Is equally interested with us, but I am sorry to say that up to the present time the matter is

still where it was and we have received no satisfaction on that point.
I wish the minister would get the information as to the two years' traffic receipts?
I shall.
Does anybody control these despatches from the other side that come by cable; I mean principally political despatches from the different countries in Europe ?
That has nothing to do with the system.
It may not have with this one, but I would like some information.

This cable is -carried on upon commercial principles, the government has nothing to do with it. The trust which sits in London which has built and manages it, carries it on on commercial principles. We have no control over the despatches which are sent over. I dare say in time of war we might exercise the power which all governments possess of seizing tlie post office and the telegraph? but in time of peace, which I hope we shall always have, although we are annually increasing our militia, there is no more control over this cable than over the cables on the Atlantic.
Then we are not much interested in this; it is more between Australia and England ?

No, the reason why (Janada went into this cable enterprise is that we want to develop the trade between Australia and Great Britain through Canada. First of all we want Australia to do her telegraphic business by this cable over Canada and we want Australia to send her goods to England over Canada. There is no reason in the world why we should not carry the whole of the passenger traffic of Australia through Canada, and I believe the time is not far distant when this will be done as we improve our communications both on the Atlantic and the Pacific. On the contrary there is every reason in the world to think that every passenger who goes from England to Australia or from Australia to England must pass though America for the reason that he would thus avoid the fatigue, annoyance and misery of a trip through the Indian ocean and the Suez canal. If a passenger leaves Australia to go to England all the time he is on or near land he is in the temperate zone, he avoids all discomforts and I have no doubt that all this will tend to the same object.
It is costly.
It has been costly.

I think there was another consideration; Canada was to contribute as the others did in order to have a line which should not pass over foreign territory and so be an all-British line. I shall not borrow any trouble with reference to that cable; I was In favour of it from the first, and I am still; I believe it will work out all right, but my right hon. friend has got to do a little hustling if he expects to see the Australian passengers going across Canada to England in this way. It must take him less than twelve years in the future to get a fast Atlantic service if he expects this.
That is part of it.

You will get Australian passengers when you can carry them to London faster than they can be carried in any other way and one means of doing that is to have a fast Atlantic service. I would like to ask the right hon. gentleman what particular business carried our Postmaster General to London at the present time. Was it in connection with this ?
Yes.
Have there been develop^ ments?

Nothing has developed; it is simply that the conditions to which I have alluded are not satisfactory at the present time in Australia. We want if possible to rectify the position which has been created by the contract given by New South Wales to the eastern company, it is partly that and partly to see how far the expenditure can be reduced, to see in what shape the commission is and to look into the matter generally.
Does Australia meet us in London?
Yes, by specially accredited agents.

I do not see how we can curtail the expenditure; we are in a
contract and are bound to carry it out.

It is our business, we are interested in it and it is part of the business to meet in London and see whether or not the expenses can be curtailed. We want to have the books examined, to see if the expenditure can be curtailed, and if the business of the company can be increased. There is one way in which we know the traffic can be increased; that is if we can get rid of the contract between New South Wales and the eastern company.
Do we vote any money for the improvement in Ottawa each year or is that statutory.
It is statutory.
Do we get any report of the expenditures?
Yes.
Yearly?
Yearly.
We have none for this year; I have been searching for it but have not been able to find it.
I am pretty sure there is a report.
That is in the Auditor General's Report.
The expenses are there, but we want more than the expenses, and I would think that when we give away $60,000 a year for fifteen years we ought to get a report each year of how this money is expended.
I am quite satisfied there is a report ; whether it has been brought down or not I do not know. [DOT]
It does not seem quite right that we should vote this as a statutory matter and get no report as to how the money is expended. Was it a condition that the city should supplement our vote?
No, the City does not supplement it.
But as a matter of fact the city does?
The city is represented on the board.
But does not supplement the vote?
No.

Then all the work which has been done by that commission is done on the basis of our 15 years' vote. Another thing that I think we ought to know is whether the commission is mortgaging more than that vote of $60,000 a year for fifteen years. I have heard it mentioned that extensive improvements are projected over and above what has been indicated, and, that in order to meet these, bonds are to be issued based upon the vote that we give. We ought to be very careful to see to it that these securities, issued to get ready money, do not cover more than the fifteen-years' vote that we give. And I think we ought to have, every year, a report from that commission as to the work done. In saying that, I am not raising any objection to the commission's work, so far as I have seen it, or to the vote. I think that the work so far as I have seen it is exceedingly well done. But it would be satisfactory to have a report, so that we might see how our money is expended.

That is most reasonable. I am sure that there is a report, and if it has not been brought down
I -will give instructions to have it produced. The statute in this matter was passed when my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) was in the House-in 1898 or 1899. At that time we provided for a ten-years' expenditure. We have amended that since, and have provided that the expenditure should be extended for fifteen years. At the same time, we have authorized the commission to issue debentures mortgaging some part of the revenues that they are to receive during these fifteen years, to enable them to purchase land. By the first statute, the commission were restricted to a certain yearly expenditure. But it was urged, and, on reflection, we thought it advisable, that the commissioners should be allowed to make purchase of lands to lay them down for parks. The idea we had in mind at that time was to allow the commission to make a large expenditure on Rockliffe Park. They were authorized to issue debentures, and they have done so. They have purchased about 80 acres of land on the bank of the Ottawa river near Rock-liffe Park and have laid it out for a park. In my opinion they should purchase double that quantity. I think all cities make the mistake of not having sufficient parks. As Ottawa will undoubtedly be a large city, a large park should be secured immediately. I shall be surprised if the report is not down, but, if necessary, I will give instructions to have it brought down.

I suppose the government takes care that securities are not issued beyond the amount voted; otherwise we may find ourselves, one of these days, with a number of fine improvements, but with a call on parliament for an extension of this vote. The vote amounts to $900,000, which is a munificent donation for the purpose. I wish to say, however, that the city ought not to feel, because of this large prospective expenditure, that it should cease its efforts or should fail to co-operate with the government to make the city what all feel that it should be made. The city ought not to rely on this vote for all its park improvements. Public spirited citizens are doing something for the extension of Ottawa's parks, at Britannia and Aylmer there are beautiful outing places which have been provided by corporations. I do not think the city ought to feel that all such great improvements will hereafter be made by the government or by corporations. I think the donation we have given is a large and generous one, and, with proper cooperation of the city and the corporations, it should do everything that is necessary for the beautification of Ottawa. Ottawa lends itself to beautification. The extension in the direction of the rifle range, in my opinion is a most excellent Idea-that is certainly a most beautiful part of the city. When the project is carried out it will make a range of driveway and park the equal of which few cities will be able to show.

I quite share my bon. friend's opinion. The city of Ottawa ought not to rely altogether on the government in these matters. At the same time, the city has a good deal to do in the way of improving such a rapidly growing city-a good deal to do upon the streets, for instance.
Yes, and it is doing it very well.
The commission, so far, has been making the driveway, which is a great addition to the attractions of the city. It is proposed to extend that driveway down to the Ottawa river at the Chaudifire.
What route will that take ?
I cannot say.
Will it come from the Experimental Farm down to the river ?
Yes.
Is the route all within the city limits ?
I do not know. Talking with one of the commissioners some time ago, I learned that their object is to reach the river, take in some of the islands in the river and make a park there.
How shall we get across ?

By bridges. I think they will not be very expensive. Another, aud, in my opinion, more important part of their project is to make a park of that portion near the range. I think it will be one of the finest parks on the continent.

There is one point that is not yet quite clear. Besides what you might call the establishment of the work, there must be maintenance from year to year. I suppose that they have to rely on the $60,000 a year for both construction and maintenance, would they not ? In the issuing of their bonds have they covered the whole of our vote, or have they taken the precaution to allow for the up-keep of the system. Or, who pays for the up-keep-is it the government, the commission, or the city ?

I do not know that that question has ever been brought to my attention. I always had it in mind that the city would have to provide for the maintenance and I have not heard any opinion to the contrary. As to the reserving a portion not covered by the debentures issued, I may say that I am informed by the Minister of Justice that these are limited to $250,-
000.

That seems to provide for maintenance.
Public works-chargeable to income-public buildings-New Brunswick, $108,000.
Is it proposed to proceed with the votes for public bridges ?
There was one item left over.

I have great faith in the ability of my hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Brodeur), but I do not think he is quite big enough to undertake the public works with the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Hyman) so near the denouement
But perhaps we could deal with some of these items for public works. We might take, for example, those for the province of Quebec.
I would much rather take some estimates for which we have the ministers here.
Well, the day after to-morrow we will have the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Hyman) here.
Are all the main estimates passed ?
I promised that we would give plenty of time to discussing the Intercolonial Railway and we propose to take that up to-morrow. In the meantime, the House is pretty thin and rather demoralized-[DOT]
The minister has been in that division for some time.

My hon. friend (Mr. Foster) is very hard to please. He insists that we shall elect a Minister of Public Works, and then he does his best to prevent us electing him. And when we propose to go on with the Public Work estimates he objects because there is no minister here.
That is what an opposition is for.

In connection with public works for New Brunswick, there is an item which was allowed to stand-the drill hall at St. John. The Minister of Militia was to give some information with regard to that, but I do not see the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Daniel) in his place just now. Perhaps we had better postpone consideration of that item until he gets back. In the meantime we will take Quebec.
I think we shall have to do the same with the Quebec items, because there does not seem to be any Quebec man now in his seat.
I told the hon. member for Beauharnois (Mr. Bergeron) that we would take up the main estimates and public works for Quebec, but he is not present.
I saw the member for Beauharnois a few moments ago, and he said he could not be in until after six o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Call it six o'clock. At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
