Harbours and rivers, Quebec-Anse a, Beaufils -extension of pier, $1,500.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. P. BEODEUE (for the Minister of Public Works).
speechtext: This vote of .$1,500 covers the estimated cost of completing the extension of the piers or retaining walls on both sides of the stream. The work was commenced in 1904-5. There was an appropriation in 1904 of $2,000. There has been expended to the 1st January, $1,458.48.
Does my hon. friend remember the first work commenced at Anse ft Beaufils? I am surprised to hear the hon. minister state that this work was only commenced in 1904.
The extension was only commenced in 1904-5, but I understand work has been going on there for some time. I see that the total amount expended has been $9,000. It began in 1887-S.
Is it a wharf ?
This is to create a harbour at the entrance of the cove and this is a kind of protection wall. The object is to enable the fishermen to get into the Anse a Beaufils without any difficulty.
Where is it ?
In Gaspe ?
On the St. Lawrence ?
Yes.
Does that finish the whole thing ?
Yes, that completes it.
Well, we will see next year. I am sure we will see an item for Anse it Beaufils again.

There may be some repairs next year.
Anse aux Gris Fonds-improvements at mouth of river, $3,500.
This vote is of the same character. This $3,500 is for continuing the improvements commenced at the mouth of the river that flows into the Anse aux Gris Fonds.
Where is that ?
Oil the Gaspe coast, on the River St. Lawrence. It is not very far from Anse 3, Beaufils.
Is that river navigable ?
No, the Anse a Beaufils is not. This is a work constructed at the mouth of the river in order to form a harbour and provide a shelter for the fishermen.
When was it commenced ?
What is the total estimated cost of the work ?
Is that given by tender ?
No, there was only $1,500 voted last year and it was done by day's work. Mr. Morin conducted the work.

Why is it that these public undertakings are done by day's work ? There is no excuse for it at all. This was a new undertaking and it should have been let by tender. Was this done about the time you were having an election ?

It is a kind of work that it is difficult to find contractors to undertake. I am informed that the department asked for some tenders at a place called Grands Mechins and that they' could not get anybody to tender.

It is a very astounding thing that you cannot get contractors to undertake work like that in that section of the country. Is that in the neighbourhood of Seven Islands where work to the extent of $60,000 has been done by day labour ?
I am informed by the officials of the department that they called for tenders for work of the same kind but unfortunately they could not get anybody to tender.

If you will vote some money for wharfs in Ontario I will venture the assertion that you will find contractors who are willing to build them.
Anse St. Jean-extension of pier, $1,000.
Where is that ?
In Chicoutimi and Saguenay, on the Saguenay. This is a vote of $1,000 chiefly for the completion of the work. There was an appropriation last year of $1,200.
But, that was spent.
Yes.
How is it that you had an appropriation of $1,200 last year and that it will cost $1,000 more to finish it V
Because the full amount was not voted last year, and it has been found that this sum Is required to complete the work.
The estimated cost last year was $1,200 ?
No, the appropriation was $1,200, but the total estimated cost was $2,200.
Will this 81.000 finish the whole work ?

Yes.
Baie des Peres, Lake Temiskaming-reconstruction of wharf at Ville Marie, including dredging approach, $2,500.
Why are we called upon to build wharfs there ? This is not on a river ?

* No, but it is on Lake Temiskaming. As my hon. friend knows there are many places where we have wharfs on Lake Temiskaming. There are many steamboats running on that lake. Baie des Peres is certainly one of the most important places on the lake.
How large is Lake Temiskaming ?
Seventy-five miles long by about four miles wide. As my hon. friend sees it covers a very extensive territory.
How could you get a dredge there ?
There is a dredge belonging to the Public Works Department on the lake.
She must have been built there.

Yes.
Barachois de Malbaie-breakwater, $4,500.
'Sir. BRODEUR. The total estimated cost is $16,000, and it is intended to call for tenders.
Where is this ?
It is Gaspe county, on the St. Lawrence.
Is jthere a /vil&agle there ?

It must be an incorporated village. The work was asked for many years ago ; there is a petition dated 1881 from the Hon. Mr. Fortin asking for a breakwater at that place. It is the centre of a large fishing trade, where sixty or seventy fishing boats are employed In the summer, and the population must be between 1,500 and 2,000.

I know the place ; I was there last summer. It is a large shoally bay, with a barachois at the entrance.
Belocil guide piers and booms-to make good damage by ice, $500.

There are piers below the Grand Trunk Railway bridge at Beloeii to facilitate the passage of steamers and barges through the narrow swing bridge, where the current is very swift. This vote it to repair the piers and booms.
Bic harbour-wharf at Poiute a Cote, $5,000.
Why has nothing been done there ?
(Because there was some difficulty with regard to the purchase of a site. No money has been spent.
Is that work very useful ?
I understand it is ; Bic is used by the pilots.

Was there not some difficulty about that work ?
Mr. BRODEUR, Not that I know of.
I think I have some correspondence about that, and I may have to ask the hon. gentleman to come back to tbe item again.
Do I understand this wharf will be built to Massacre Island ?
Yes, from a point eastward.
Will you interfere with the present high-tide approach to the existing wharf ?

No.
Canton Fabre, Lake Temiskaming-wharf,$2,-
000.
Where is that ?
The item is prepared according to the estimate of the chief engineer for the construction of a wharf on lot 31, township of Fabre.
Will this he reached by the new railroad ?

No ; this is on the east side, in the province of Quebec.
iMr. AMES. I understand the Canadian Pacific Railway contemplates building a branch on the east side.
air. BRODEUR. I am informed that it is forty-five miles away from the railroad. It is in the county of Pontiac.
air. AMES. Would any considerable population be served by that wharf ? It is a long and narrow lake, and the steamers stop practically anywhere and put passengers off on either side of the lake in the ship's jolly-boat. Unless there is some population, there is no use in building this wharf.

When air. Tarte was Minister of Public Works he visited Lake Teinis-camingue, and a large deputation waited on him to represent the need for a wharf at that point, and he promised that it would be built. The shores are very bluff, and in a high wind it is nearly impossible to land with the jolly-boat from the steamer. The only means of access they have in summer is by steamer.
'What is the population ?
There must be at least 200 families within reasonable reach of the wharf.
What do you mean by reasonable reach ?
Within a radius of four or five miles.
Is It a farming poipulation ?
Yes.
I suppose the freight will be (mostly bulky material, such as hay, which could not be taken in the jolly-boat.
Yes ; and getting in lumbermen's supplies.

When did Mr. Tarte promise to build this -wharf ?
(Mr. McCOOL. It is not in my county ; it is in the county of Pontiac ; but I happened to be present when the deputation waited on Mr. Tarte. It was two or three years ago.
The hon. gentleman's memory is not very good when he cannot tell within a year.

In works like these at Bie harbour and Canton Fa'ure, it would look as if they were promised on the eve of the election last year ; and now that the election is over, I do not suppose there will be much need for them.

I do not think that is correct. There was a petition some years ago asking for the wharf, and a vote was put in the estimates last year, but there is a difference of opinion amongst the settlers as to whether it should be at Lavallge bay or Quinn point, and no decision has yet been reached.
Chambord wharf, $2,500.
This is to complete payment on the contract. The conttract was for $9,250. It was given to the lowest tender, Mr. Arthur Tremblay, of Roberval.
Why do you want $10,500 ?
$1,250 are for superintendence and contingencies.
We think an architect's charge of five per cent quite ample for the construction of a house. Why should the charge for building a wharf be greater ?
There are other things and ten per cent is the amount always allowed.
Is it not an employee of the government who is in charge ?
Yes, Mr. Tachfi, and then there is a Icoal inspector, Mr. A. Le-may, who gets $2.50 a day and'the expenses of these gentlemen have to be paid also going from place to place.
Why not include the contingencies in the first amount and make one item ?

We have always thought it better to give the contractor's price in one item and the supplementary expenses in the other.
Champlain, Quebec-wharf repairs and additional, $2,000.

This is to complete the wharf at that place. The work is done by day labour. The estimated cost was $8,200. We spent only $6,200 and require $2,000 to spend during the next fiscal year. This is no increase but simply a revote. This work is done by day labour because it is the repairs to an old wharf and is better done In that way than by contract. It was almost impossible to specify what work has to be done. It will be finished by about September.
Chateau Richer-harbour improvements, $6,-
000.

This is the balance required for improvements made by day labour, namely, the removal of rocks on the bar and the construction of a breakwater, the appropriation was $9,000. Chateau Richer is in Montmorency county.
What kind of boats go there ?

Vessels carrying firewood, iron and other material and bringing [DOT]return cargoes of supplies of all kinds. The total number of schooners and bateaux at that place last year was 35 with the total carrying capacity of 3,500 tons.
Will you make the wharf longer than it is now ?
No.

How does it come that although a wharf was built there years and years ago and the people have always used that wharf, you have this year to spend so much money at that place? 1 suppose there was no election there?

Trade I understand has been increasing and they require some more accommodation. The cargoes carried by these vessels last year were valued at $50,-
000.	My friend will see it is not a useless expenditure.

Is that on the Island
of Orleans?
No, it is on the mainland.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The importance of this place has increased lately because of the valuable stone quarries there. Stone is taken from there for the harbour improvements at Quebec.

Could not the people who have a quarry there build a wharf for themselves ? It is easy for them to come to the government and ask them to build a wharf because they want to carry stone from that place. You might just as well give the monev to a farmer. If a farmer goes to the west and has to buy a horse or two, a wagon and harness, you might as well rig him out with these things as to rig these fellows out with a wharf. Is that the case or not?
This work was constructed many years ago. It was commenced in 1SS4-5.

And before that too.
Mr. BROOK UR, The note I have here gives that date and it is simply carrying out the same policy as was adopted by the former government. I do not think it would be good policy to let these works fall into decay; I do not suppose my hon. friend would recommend that.

I do not see how that would happen. I have shipped from that wharf, and it must be remembered that the tide has to rise about eight feet before the water reaches the wharf ; you cannot load or unload unless the tide is away up and when the tide is down the water is half a mile from the wharf. It is not a great place for business there and I do not see why a wharf is so much required.

If my hou. friend has been shipping there himself, he must understand that it is a useful work, and he must admit too that there are in that section of the country wharfs which have been built which cost a great deal more than this work, and I do not think there should be any objection to such a sanall amount as has been spent there in comparison with the amounts spent in some other places. My friend knows that other places have beeii asking for wharfs reaching to low tide and we have been spending large sums of money. There is no comparison between the amounts spent in those places and the small amount sjient in this place. There is a great deal of trade there, the extensive quarries are being exploited and I think it is a very useful expenditure which has been petitioned for by the inhabitants of the place.
I would like to have the name of the foreman, the amount that was paid, the rate of wages that was paid to him and to the men, the number of men employed, and where the material was got.
The foreman was Ed. Vezina, 1 shall get the other information.
When was the work commenced?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: Last year, in July or August.
It was done during the election time, as a matter of fact.

I suppose so ; the appropriation was voted last year and would become available some time in July or August and the work would then be commenced. If the elections happened to take place in that time of course the work must have been going on.
I am not making any insinuations at all; I am only mentioning the fact that the work was done during the election.

I recollect distinctly that on a job of this kind there was a foreman attending to the construction of the work, a gentleman employed in buying the timber, and another gentleman who got so much per cent of the money invested in purchasing the material. The minister would not say I am sure that in a job like this it would be hard to get the material by contract. It becomes serious when you have a lot of officials and hangers-on about election time) when you have a job of this kind going on month after month and year after, year with a lot of men employed at big wages.
I am informed this is going to complete the work.

I never complain about where money is spent as long as it is properly spent, but I do not think that any minister or any official of the minister can get the work doue as well as it can be done by contract. And it is of no use to teli me or to tell this committee that it is impossible, either in Quebec or any other place in Canada, to get the material by contract. Here is a work, that, as I understand it, is on dry land when the tide is out, but is reached bv the sea when the tide is high. Are the men able to work when the tide is in? If not, are they paid just the same?

The wharf is not submerged at high tide, but at high tide the water reaches the wharf. In many places wharfs are built so that vessels reach them at low water, but this one is built so that it is reached only at high water, and it is so built for the sake of economy. It is one of the least expensive works in that section and for that reason.

I understand that this wharf is being completed by day labour. How does the minister get over the Act of parliament that declares that all works over $5,000 shall be done by contract? Under what authority does the minister presume to do this by day's work. Of course, I do not hold the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Brodeur) responsible for this, as I suppose that it was not under his
direction that the construction was undertaken. But lie is here to defend the action of the Minister of Public Works. This is another of the many cases in which ministers come down and tell us that they are constructing public works by day labour though the Act explicitly says that such works shall be done by contract. What explanation has the minister to give for the conduct of the department on this occasion ?

Perhaps I did not make myself very clear in my opening remarks. There are two kinds -of work to be paid for under this vote. One is the removal of rocks. My hon. friend knows that such work cannot be very well done by contract, because it is not easy to ascertain how much work will be required. I understand that it is impossible to find contractors who will undertake such work for a fixed amount. Then there is the work on the breakwater pier. This is not all construction, but includes also repairs, and this kind of work it. is almost impossible to have done by day's labour. And this is not a violation of tiie law. The Public Works Act provides that works over $5,000 shall be done under contract. But the same law provides that if the work can be more effectively done by day labour, it shall be done in that way. This is an instance.

The minister may be right. 1 have not the statute before me. But I shall be very much surprised if there is a provision in the Act such as he has suggested-that it is left by the minister to have the work done by day's labour if he thinks it is desirable to do so. I certainly have not so understood the law. I have always understood that where the expenditure is over $5,000, the work must be done under contract. X have before me the proposed amendment to the law which provides that the minister shall invite tenders for public-works, unless there is an emergency in which delay would be injurious to the public interest, or the work can be more efficiently and expeditiously done by the officers of the department, or in case the estimated cost is less than $5,000, or where it appears to the minister that it is not advisable to invite tenders. It may be to this proposed amendment that the minister refers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, that makes the law more stringent than it is.

I would like to know how the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) interprets this law? If I am mistaken in what I have always supposed to be file law, til'sn it would appear that parliament has practically no protection. From what the minister (Mr. Brodeur) tells us, if the work involved an expenditure of $100,000, the minister would be as much within the law in doing it by day's work if the amount involved was less than $5,000.
That is done in some cases

We regret to see that it is so in many cases. I hope the Minister of Justice will have the law amended to make it more stringent; because the only protection we have is that thers should be competition in works of this kind,
Under this amendment, it would not even be necessary for the minister to go to the Governor in Council for their approval. That simply means that the whole thing is a farce.

There are cases in which it is impossible to have work done by contract. There are parts of the country where the contractors will not tender for such work as this, as they cannot estimate the cost. And there are cases where works constructed by day labour have been found cheaper than they could possibly have been had they been done under contract. There is no intention on the part of the department to evade the law. But, where the work cannot be advantageously done by contract, it is done by day labour. The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) asked me to quote the law. It is found in the Revised Statutes of 18S6, section 13 :
The minister shall invite tenders, by public advertisement, for the execution of all works except in cases of pressing emergency in which delay would be injurious to the public interest, or in which, from the nature of the work, it can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and servants of the department.
Is there any evidence that it can be more expeditiously done by officers of tbe department than by contract .

That is a question for the department to decide. This is not a question of construction, it is a question of repairs ; and the hon. member knows that it is almost impossible to make specifications in regard to repairs. You must have some construction first before you can make any repairs to it.

We are not arguing that all work must be done by contract; in many cases of repairs it would be impossible to liave them done by contract. But this is a new work attached to au old work *, in other words, this is an extension of a pier, it is an entirely new piece of work, and therefore it should be done by contract.

It is the removal of rocks. I am informed by the officer of the department that it is found much more economical to have that work done by day labour than by contract. It would he impossible, almost, to get anybody to tender.
Are you removing rocks from a bill ?
From the bar opposite the village. Vessels were iiable to strike the rock, and it was thought advisable to remove that rock in order to give better transportation facilities.

From the wharf out to the channel is about three-quarters of a mile, and you have rocks and boulders all the way across from the wharf to the channel ; and then there is a bar above the wharf that extends for miles with nothing but rocks and boulders.
Then my hon. friend sees the need of removing these rocks for the protection of the road.
Is that the only thing you have to do, to remove the rocks and boulders ?
And repair the break-tv a ter pier.
Is this harbour owned by the government, or is it private property ?
The work done so far has been done by the government. This work was begun in 1884.
Is the property vested in the Crown ?

Yes.
Mi-. BLAIN. When was it purchased, and how much was paid ?
I have not got the information here. The work was begun in 1884, perhaps the records have been destroyed by the fire. All harbours are vested in the Crown.

This matter was up several times before, and I notice that a considerable amount has been appropriated each year to purchase these properties from private individuals. When this very item was up for discussion last year my hon. friend from Halton asked the question :
Is this vested in the Crown, or is it private property ?

Probably it will he vested in the Crown. The actual deed has not passed but an agreement has been made for the purchase from a private individual.
It is fair now that the minister should tell us what amount was paid for this property, and the name of the persons who owned the property.
I am informed by the officers of the department that an approach has been purchased. That is the reason why that statement was made last year.
I would ask if the agreement referred to last year by the minister has been carried out, has the property been pui chased, and is it now vested in the Crown ?
Will the government receive any revenue from that wharf ?
Y'es, the law provides for certain charges to be made at these wharfs.

I like to see a government clever, but there is such a thing as being too clever. Now the government has given subsidies to build a railway from Quebec, and they are giving more money to build wharfs and remove rocks. I may tell the minister that the railway goes right over the wharf twenty feet from the water. There should be an end to these things. I am willing to help people who need to be helped but those people have a railway there and that railway goes right past the quarry. Thev had even to dig down to the wharf to build this railway because there was a heavy grade there. The railway almost touches the wharf. When these people have a railway for their accommodation what is the use of going to the expense of building a wharf ?
Is that a steam railway ?

It used to be a steam railway. Now they are operating the same road by steam and electricity. They run electric cars every ten minutes in the day in the summer time and in the winter time they run steam cars about every hour in the day.

My hon. friend knows the locality very well and he knows that most of the traffic that is carried on there is carried on by means of schooners. It is quite true there is an electric railway built nearby, but most of the traffic is carried on by schooners. Most of the traffic is between Quebec and the south shore of the St. Lawrence. My hon. friend knows that there is no bridge connecting there. My hon. friend who lives oil the south shore has told us that he has been shipping from his place to that point.

I said that I shipped to and from there, but not from my own place.
I shipped from the north shore.
My hon. friend knows that there is some traffic on the south shore.
Yes.
And that it is necessary to have a wharf ?

That is perfectly right, but I am opposed to giving too much to the same people. Somebody else needs a railway or a wharf or a bridge or the help of the government. I always have objected and 1 will object as long as I am a member of

this House to favouring oue man and crushing another. This money belongs to one man as much as it does to another, and everybody, as far as it is in the power of the government, should be protected. If the government have 8100.000 to give let them give it but not give it all to one man. Let everybody have his share. That is nothing more than right.
Equal rights.

Yes, Sir. We had the promise from the right hon. leader of the government in 1S95 that when he got into power his government would be a government of reform and a government of example. I am looking for the example, but I have not seen it yet, and I hope the" government will never display it.
That is not a fair hope.
Well, it is politics. It is all very well to make promises and then never fulfil them.
What was the object of purchasing that piece of land my hon. friend spoke of buying a little while ago ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It was to get access from the high road. My hou. friend knows the conditions that exist at Chateau Richer. This is a place below Montmorency Falls. The adjoining parish is I/Ange Gar-dien, the next is Chateau Richer and the next is Ste. Anne de Beauprf*. They have a stone quarry on the north side in the main road and in order to get down to this harbour which has been a harbour within my recollection for the last fifty years, they have to cross from the main road through the property of this man Guiguere to get to the wharf.
How did they get to the wharf before that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I suppose they trespassed upon this property. The wharf has been extended as a result of these improvements and the improvements in the trade of the place. This particular place is the centre of two great industries. It is a great place for quarries and in addition they export an immense quantity of fire-wood. I suppose that two-thirds of the fire wood, that goes to Quebec comes from Chateau Richer. All that fire wood comes in bateaux from that place. My hon. friends know that the tide rises and falls there for It to IS feet and in order to get that wood out of there it is necessary for the bateaux to go into the wharf.
When was that land bought ?
Within the last four or five months. The deputy minister does not remember at this moment the exact date.
That would be in December or January ?
Yes.
Can you not tell when the property was bought ?
The deputy minister will find that out for the hon. gentleman.

It seems extraordinary that you cannot tell when the property was bought. There must be a deed. You must find out when that property was bought. If this has been an important harbour for fifty years and it was found necessary five mouths ago to buy some property it does seem extraordinary, and we are entitled to get that information. I would ask my hon. friend to take a note of it and give us all the information.

Yes.
Desjardins-Allumette Island-River Ottawa- wharf, $1,000.
This is to complete. It is under contract.
Where is that ?
On the Ottawa river not very far from Pembroke.
Which county ?
Pontiac.
If I am not making a mistake this is a revote ?
Yes.
The amount of money to be spent on that wharf will be $11,000; $10,000 could only be spent to the first of July and the rest is a revote. That is proof of economy.
Yes, we are trying to do what my hon. friend from Dorchester (Mr. Morin) says.

The hon. member from Dorchester is right.
Mr. dRODEUR. I will not go as far as that.
Doucet's Landing-dredging, $15,000.

This vote covers the estimated cost of forming a basin 800 feet long, 450 feet wide and 13 feet deep at low water on the east side of the railway wharf at Doucet's Landing of the Arthabaska and Three Rivers branch of the Grand Trunk Railway, where steamboats calling at this landing can remain safely at anchor during stormy weather.
We voted some money for this the other day.
It was to pay for work done during the current year. This is for next year. Tenders have been called for this work.
What will be the cost of the whole work ?
$15,000 will complete it.
How much was spent before ?
The total expenditure for many years back has been $39,000.
What was spent last year ?
We voted $8,000 the other day in the supplementary estimates.
That was to pay for work done during the current fiscal year.
Do you mean to say you spent $20,000 in one year ?
Yes, for dredging.
And $15,000 more; that will be $35,000.
$35,000. The work is being done by contract.
Who is doing that ?
The work has been awarded to Mr. Randolph McDonald.
Were there any other tenders ?
Yes ; and he was the lowest tenderer.
Did Mr. Randolph Macdonald have the same advantages that were given to the contractor in the Port Arthur case 1
Yes ; public tenders were called for, and he was the lowest tenderer and got the work.
At what price ?
Nine cents .per cubic yard.	_
What is the material to be dredged ?
Gravel and boulders.

We were told by the Solicitor Genei-al the other night that the dredging was to remove sand, and I pointed out that it would be futile to go on dredging sand year after year unless you put in some protection work to prevent the sand from chifting back.
It would cost more to do that.
It might cost more at first, but it would be cheaper in the end. How much money has been spent at this place ?
The total amount expended was $39,334.62 to the 31st December, 1904.
Mx-. BERGERON. And in addition to that we have the $8,000 and the $15,000 now, which makes over $62,000.
Yes.
Will this complete the work ?
Yes.
And when you have the work done, what kind of boats can use the wharf ?
Boats having a less draught than 13 feet.
Why did the government discontinue dredging by the hour and substitute by the cubic yard ?
Because of a discussion iu the House it was thought better to call for public Tenders and have the work done in this way.
How many tenders were there ?
Three ; one at 9 cents, one at 15 cents and one at 22 cents.
Did the government pay for the towing of the dredge from Cornwall to Doucet's landing ?
No ; Mr. Macdonald had extensive works on the north shore, and the reason his tender is so low is that he will take the material from the south shore and use it for filling on the north shore.

Is this wharf to be used by a railway company ?
Mr. iBRODEUR. The wharf there (is owned by the Grand Trunk.
Does the Grand Trunk Railway contribute anything ?
No ; this vote is for dredging, and is not for the wharf.
Some years ago Mr. Tarte told the House that the dredging in the St. Lawrence could be done for three cents per cubic yard, and now you are paying Mr. Macdonald nine cents.

Mr. Tarte was referring to a very powerful new dredge called the ' J. I. Tarte,' which works iu clay, but this work is in gravel and boulders, and besides we could not expect that a contractor should have such au extraordinary dredge as the one owned toy the government.

I uiudeustand you very plainly now.
East Templeton wharf, $6,500.
How much is this wharf going to cost altogether 1
$6,500. This is a revote; nothing has been done.
Is this wharf used very much toy the public, and will there be any revenue from it ?
There is a wharf there uow belonging to the Ottawa Navigation C-ompany, and it is intended to get that wharf for the use of the public.
Does the government propose to buy this wharf from the Navigation Company ?
It was the intention, in order to make it a public wharf.
Well
I made a mistake ; I am told that the wharf is to be transferred from the Navigation Company to the government, and the government will make the necessary repairs and have the wharf for public use.
If it is in the same condition now as it was when I last saw it, it is in a very bad state of repair.

The result of this would be that the Ottawa Navigation Company would get a new wharf built by the government without any expense to themselves. This wharf has been in existence for a great many years, and it appears to have been satisfactory to the people for what small use they made of it. A certain amount of business has always been done by the public at that wharf.
The company wants to have the prior use of the wharf, but the department will not accept it on that condi-Uon, and negotiations are pending. Perhaps there will be no final result.
In what county is it ?
In the county of Wright, a few miles from here.

It seems to be the policy of the government to build many more wharfs than they formerly did. East Templeton wharf did well enough in the old days. Before undertaking to build new wharfs, does the department have any report to show what use will be made of them by the public and the expected revenue in each case ?
Yes, a report is made by the officers of the department in each case before any money is voted.

On March 6th last, I asked the acting Minister of Public Works (Mr. Hyman) a question with regard to two wharfs on the Ottawa, from neither of which was the revenue sufficient to warrant the expenditure of public money. One was at Greece's point, comity of Argenteuil, on which was spent $5,452.19. Last year the gross revenue was $60.93. Then there is the wharf at Hull, across the river, built by the government at a cost of $54,000, which
last year was used by only some ten boats, and for the use of which no wharfage is charged. I have passed this wharf a great many times and have never seen it used until a couple of days ago when I saw a small row boat landing at it. While the building of wharfs is very necessary when required for the public convenience, iu many cases they are built where they are not needed by the public at all. With regard to the wharf at East Templeton, has the hon. minister any report to show that it will be used by any company other than the Ottawa River Company, which is quite well able to take care of its own wharfs.

I am informed by the chief engineer that a report was made in the usual way before the appropriation was asked for last year. With regard to the two wharfs to which the hon. gentleman refers, they are not under the control of the Public Works Department.
On the 6th March, 1 asked a question about the wharf at Greece's point, and it was answered by the acting Minister of Public Works.

The chief engineer says that this wharf is under the control of the Department of Railways and Canals. The one at Hull was built by the Public Works Department. The other one is in connection with the canal.
How much revenue does the hon. gentleman expect from this wharf, according to the report, and what use will be made of it by the public outside the Ottawa Navigation Company ?

The department has no information on that point because the revenue is collected by the Department of Marine and Fisheries ; hut I am sure, from the information we have, that the revenue will be sufficient to meet the interest on the expenditure.
Then it will be very different from these other two wharfs on the Ottawa. The oue that cost some $5,000 gives $60 revenue, and the one that cost $54,000. gives uo revenue.
Have the company and the government come to any agreement?

Nothing has been decided between the company and the government, the transfer has not been made yet by the Ottawa Navigation Company, and negotiations are going on between the department and the company. The company wants the prior use of that wharf so that they would he entitled to order any boat away which might be there when they wanted to use it, but the department did not consent.
Will this money be spent if no satisfactory arrangement is come to?
No, we will not spend anything before the transfer is made to the department.
The wharf should certainly not be built if any preference is to be given the company.
That is'why no money has been spent so far in connection with that wharf.
How have the public managed at East Templeton up to date?
They were using Mac-laren's wharf.
So that this wharf has not been used at all?
Yes, by the Ottawa Navigation Company.
Is it fit to be used?
Well, it is being used by the company.
Does the government allow7 steamboats to use a -wharf which is dangerous to the public?

We have no control over that. The company takes all the risk itself, and will be responsible for any accident.
Mr. BDA1N. Would the minister lay on the table the report under which he proposes to purchase the wharf?

Certainly.
Escoumain wharf, $8,000.

This is to provide for building a public pier, which is under contract. The cost altogether will be $11,478, and the usual amount for superintendence and contingencies, $1,522.	$10,000 were
voted and $5,000 of that is a revote, so we will be spending only $5,000 and $8,00u or $13,000.
Gatineau Point-repairs to wharf and to retaining wall above it, $1,100.
This expenditure is to be made on a retaining wall for shore protection built some fifty years ago. It is being done by day labour.
Do any steamboats stop at the wharf at this place ?
This is for repairs to the retaining wall.
Are we bound to keep) it in repair ?

Yes, because it is built by ourselves.
Grands Mechins breakwater, $20,000.

This is a work for wTiic-h tenders have been called but nobody has tendered. It is for the construction of Mr. BERGERON.
a breakwater here, extending 603 feet from the eastern side of the harbour of Grand Mechins to afford better protection. This is in Rimouski county, fifty-four miles from Little Metis and eighty miles from Rimouski.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: $5,000 has already been spent.
$5,000 was spent during tlie wTinter for timber. We called for tenders and nobody would make any tender, but we had to buy the lumber aud it has been delivered during the last winter.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Are you calling for tenders again ?
We will call for tenders again.

By whom will the harbour that will be formed by this work he used, by the local fishermen and traders or will this accommodate the larger vessels that pass down the northern Gaspfi coast such as the ' Oampaua ' and the ' King Edward ' ?
It will be for the fishermen and for the general trade. This will provide a depth of 171 feet and will be sufficient, the chief engineer informs me, to accommodate vessels such as the 'Campana.'

If it is purely a local expenditure for the protection of the fishermen it is a large amount, but if it makes a harbour sufficient for the * Campana ' it is a national expenditure and a considerable sum might be permitted.

The object is to afford shelter to the fishermen and also landing and shipping accommodation. The only railway connection these peop>le have is the Intercolonial Railway which passes Little Metis fifty-four miles from there, so those people have no accommodation at all.

As the minister well knows that coast is not served by railway, but by steamers passing up and down and also by the local trading schooners. There are times frequently, when there is a southeasterly wind, when it is impossible for vessels, even of the size of the 1 Campana,' to take on freight from the shore, especially when barrels of cod oil, one of the large exports from that district, are being taken on board. If this affords a protected roadstead in which large vessels of the size of the ' Campana ' can enter and load in comparatively still water then it is a worthy expenditure, but if it will not assist in any way the trade of the coast and is only to be used to protect the fishermen or a few vessels loading timber, it is a large expenditure.
The object is to afford protection to vessels like the ' Campana.'
Then it would be better for the government if necessary to make an expenditure of $5,000 more in order to make an inclosed harbour 17i feet deep.
As a matter of fact tile estimated cost is $30,000. We are simply asking $20,000 but shall have to ask a further sum. This is the amount supposed to be spent during the coming year.
There is no harbour from Rimouski to GaspC where vessels the size of the ' Campana ' can enter.

There is not. And there have been some cases where there has been great danger in storms to steamers passing up and down. If a harbour can be obtained for $25,000 or $30,000 the expenditure is legitimate if it will afford a port with sufficient depth of water to enable vessels to load and unload in safety.

How long a roadstead will you have with a depth of 174 feet ? That depth will be all right provided you have it for a length of 500 or 600 feet along the pier, but if you have it only on the face of the breakwater that will not help you very much.

I am informed that the depth will be from 12 feet to 174 feet for a length of about 500 feet along the pier.
Grosse Isle quarantine station-extension of landing pier to deep water, $10,000.

This is an amount asked for by the Department of Agriculture in connection with the quarantine. It is to make provision for the extension of the west or landing pier of Grosse Isle to secure a depth of 30 feet at low water, spring tide, along the face. This will allow the largest ships entering the St. Lawrence to reach the wharf at any stage of the tide.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: This is a revote ?

Yes, nothing has been spent.
Quebec-harbours, rivers and bridges-general repairs and improvements, $25,000.

This is to cover the cost of repairs to piers, bridges, &c., where they become necessary- as well as to provide for the travelling expenses of resident engineers in the province of Quebec during the year. The amount spent last y-ear under this head was $19,477.77.

I do not know whether the Department of Public Works have received a request from the parish of St. Timotliee. in the county of Beauharnois. There is a wharf there built by the government many years ago and the keeping of which in repair is also the business of the government. But it has been allowed to fall into very had condition. I understood that a promise had been made that it would be repaired. The authorities there were to have communicated with the department, but I do not know whether that has been done or not. But I would ask If the repairs of this
wharf could not be carried out under this vote. They would not cost very much.
How much ?

I suppose $1,000 would put the work in very good shape. At present it is in a dangerous condition.
Mr. BRODEUR, The officers of the department advise me that they have not received any information on the matter. But they will take note of the case and the department will look into it.
Lake St. John-dredging, $4,000.
Where is the dredging being done ?
At the mouth of the river at Roberval and other places on Lake St. John.
Can the hon. minister say at what other places ?
At the mouth of the three different rivers, the Metabetchouan, the Peribonka and the Mistassini.
Does the dredge belong to the government ?	*
Yes, and this is to pay the running expenses of the dredge.

If I remember well, the dredging is .to remove the sandbars at the mouths of these rivers. Is the government able to hold the work that it has done ? Having dredged a channel, what steps do the government take to make the work permanent ?
I am informed that the channels are held with difficulty. In the supplementary estimates there will be an item for the construction of retaining piers.

The government will have to do that, for it is mere waste of money to dredge without building retaining piers, particularly at the Grand Discharge.
Laprairie-ice piers and protection walls- works of reconstruction and repairs, $5,000.
This is to complete the work under contract.
Who has this contract?
Messrs. Amyot and Le-may of Montreal.
What was the amount of the vote ?

Their contract was for $29,650.
Lavaltrie-pile wharf and dredging, $5,000.

What depth of water will be had there ?
Mr. BRODEUR, This is for the boats of the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Com-I pany running between Montreal and Charn-



bly. The depth will be from ten to twelve feet.
Le Tableau, Descente des Femmes-wharf on River Saguenay, $6,000.

This covers works to be executed at Descente des Femmes, the completion of a wharf on the north shore of the Saguenay river. The wharf has to be sheeted with four-inch plank and a portion of the floor is to be completed.

There are several
wharfs on the Saguenay. In which parish is this ?
It is on the north side and about fifty miles below Ha, Ha, bay.
Is it a new wharf ?
Yes.

Is there a parish
there ?
There is a village there -a new settlement and a progressive one. They have no' other means of communication than by this wharf.
Is that to be done by day's work ?
Yes.
What wages do you pay labourers in the Saguenay district ?
$2.50 for foremen, and $1.25 to $1.40 to others.
When was the $1,000 spent ?

The work was begun last year. There is a mistake in this item. Instead of being $0,000 it should be $000. It is an error in the printing.
Little Pabos-harbour improvements, $4,000.
Mr. BRODEUR, This is to make further provision for extending 100 feet in a westerly direction the breakwater built in 1889, in order to afford shelter to the fishing boats that frequent the locality. It is at the mouth of the river.

That river is subject to great floods in the spring, and a breakwater built there would need to be carefully made.
L'lle d'Alma-removal point of rock, $1,000.
This is to remove by blasting some rocks which obstruct navigation. It is in the county of Chicoutimi, on the river of that name.

It is very strange that the government should spend money at that place. There is a ridge of rocks in the river, and the government proposes to blast the rocks so as to make the river wider. If the government is going to make canals of all the rivers, streams, creeks and brooks in Mr. BRODEUR.
the country, they have a big job before them.
Lower St. Lawrence-removal of rocks, &e., $3,000.

This is the ordinary vote taken every year. It is proposed to spend this money in the counties of GaspS and Bonaventure.
Magdalen Islands-breakwaters and piers,

This is to make provision. in accordance with the estimate, for carrying on, during the coming fiscal year, projected works in connection with breakwaters, piers and wharfs in the Magdalen Islands, with a view to affording better shelter and harbour facilities, not only to a large number of fishing vessels, but also to steam sailing vessels and row-boats, and the coasting trade and fishing industry of the lower St. Lawrence.
You spent $20,000 last year and $20,000 is asked for this year. Does that cover all the work to be done ?
Yes. The chief part of this work is to be done on the islands of Pointe fi Elie, Grindstone, Bassin and Albright. These wharfs are being extended and deepened.

The other day I understood from the Solicitor General that on account of the sandbar between the island of Amherst there is only one place where vessels of a certain dimension can go. There is enough water on both sides of the island for large steamers.
I am informed that they slop at Pointe il Elie, Grindstone and Bassin.
They generally get a tender to go ashore.
That was when there were no wharfs.

What is the object of this 1 Is it for large navigation or particularly for the fishermen ?
(Mr. BRODEUR. It is for large navigation. It is in order to connect these islands with the outside world.
Do large boats ply between the Magdalen Islands and other ports ? .
There is a regular ferry from Pictou to these islands. Besides there Is provision for sailing boats and large fishing boats.
How many boats are there plying between the islands and Pictou ?
There is only one ferry.
Is that every day ?
Every week; perhaps twice a week. I am not sure.
Is there just one vessel ?
There is a direct line between Pictou and the Magdalen Islands.
What other vessels are there ?

What is this expenditure for ?

Is that dredge kept there all the time ?
Yes.
Since when ?

The dredge has been there for several years. This is to improve that part of the St. Maurice river which is navigable for SO miles, between La Tuque and Grande Piles. There are sandbars which form at different places, and the only way to remove them, in order to enable the logs to come down and the boats to get through and allow- the lumbermen to get in their supplies, is by dredging. There is another item in the estimates for the building of a dam, and when this dam is built, it w-ill raise the water and do away with the necessity for the dredging in that part of the St. Maurice river.

The work at Nieolet and Chateauguay seems to be similar to this. I am not criticising this vote, but I think it would be better to do some permanent work there than to be constantly spending money in dredging, w-hich has to be repeated year after year.

River St. Maurice-dam at Grande Piles, $19,-
000.

This vote will provide for the construction of a dam 940 feet long at the head of the Grande Piles falls, w-ith the object of increasing the boom area in order to afford accommodation for the continually increasing cut of logs on the St. Maurice river and its tributaries.

Mr. BEItGBROX. Why was this work not commenced last year ?

They have been taking soundings which is very difficult work at that particular spot, and it took considerable time before a decision could be arrived at as to what kind of a dam would be built. We have the report of the engineers, and soundings have been made in different places during the last two years. This year plans are ready and have been submitted to the department.
How much will it cost ?
I believe the estimate is $50,000 or $60,000.
Will this dam do away with the necessity of constantly dredging the river between Grande Piles and La Tuque ?

The object of the dam is threefold. In the first place, it will back up the waters for eighteen miles and make the river navigable, in the second place, it will afford accommodation for storing the legs, and I may say that within a few years the capacity of the St. Maurice river has increased from one-half million pieces to six million pieces this year. They have now no place in the river to store these logs, and the further back they have to go in order to get the logs the longer it takes to get them down to the mills. If there is no storage for these logs in the river, then the result will be that the cut of this year could not be got out until next year. Proper storage for the logs would moi'e than double the producing capacity of the St. Maurice river. In the third place, below Grande Piles the water is sometimes too low in summer for the drive, and the mills have to suspend work. The river is shallow and full of rocks in that place. This dam will raise the water and facilitate the driving of the logs. It will also do away with the necessity for dredging, it will increase the capacity of the St. Maurice river and facilitate the driving of logs.
Who are the lumbermen interested in this?

There are quite a number of lumber concerns on the river. l cannot tell you all from memory. There is the St. Maurice Lumber Company, the Gres Falls Lumber Company, Alexander Baptist, the Burrlll Lumber Company, the Union Bag and Paper Company, the Laur-entide Paper Company, the Belgo-Canadian Pulp and Paper Company, the Burgess Sulphite Fibre Company. Do I understand this is to cost $60,000?
Mr. BUREAU, i think it will cost more than that.
It seems to me that we are spending this $70,000 to help the lumber companies.
They are paying for it.

In boom and slide dues.
We would get that revenue anyway from them.
I do not think so.

1 have no doubt that these great lumbermen contribute in a variety of ways to the national revenue; I contribute myself, we all contribute. But, the question is whether it would be proper for the government to contribute to this work, which is for the benefit of private property. It is admitted it will cost $70,000. My hon. friend said it would improve the navigation to the extent of eighteen miles at that point, but navigation there extends over ninety miles. We should certainly obtain some assistance from the lumber company.
I thought my hon. friend wauted everything free?

I never urged that. What I said is that a lot of these expenses should be cut down and the money spent on perfecting our transportation system. It is unfair, when we require to spend so much on that system, that we should sacrifice nearly $100,000 to advance private interests.

Every log that goes down to the St. Lawrence contributes to the revenue of the government. We had eighty steamers last season which came to Three Rivers to load deals manufactured at our mills, and should this dam be built double this number of steamers could take their cargoes of deals at Three Rivers, but the hou. gentleman thinks they should go to Montreal. He says that this ought to be paid by the lumbermen. Not at all, every log that comes through the slides and is stored on the St. Maurice river, is an addition to the revenue of the country. The lumbermen have agreed that if the cost of this dam is more than represented by the saving in dredging and the increase of revenue, from the greater output, they will contribute.

I expressed no such desire as to bring this trade to Montreal, but I do pretend that the money would be expended to much better purpose in improving our transportation system. This expenditure is for the benefit of a lumber company, and when it comes to building a dam which will cost $100,000 and afterwards have to be maintained by the government
We will be getting a revenue.
Yes, but we are spending largely already In the interest of that locality. That the lumbermen should contribute to this work made in their interest is only fair.

When the hon. gentleman speaks of private interests he should bear in mind that there are very large industries in that section of the country which have become developed to a wonderful extent during the last ten years.
I understood that this expenditure was for the purpose of facilitating the bringing down of logs.

Yes, the erection of that dam would have the effect of increasing the lumber industry in that vicinity. To-day the situation is not absolutely favourable to the driving of logs in that section of the country. The water is rather shut off and at some seasons of the year it is difficult to drive the logs. It is expected that by the construction of this work, the driving of the logs, will become a certainty and can be made at all seasons of the year and that consequently au increased business will be done in that section of the country. This dam is also going to raise the level of the water in that section. To-day we have to spend $12,000 a year for dredging there. We expect by the construction of this dam that this work yvill not be necessary. It is a very good piece of work. Besides that my hon. friend says it Is going to benefit a private interest. He calls the millions of money invested in those works private interest. Besides that we draw a revenue which is going to increase from year to year. Last year and the year previous we got $29,000.
That is less than we expended for ordinary yearly charges and repairs.

There is one view of the case where we get some revenue out of the expenditures, and I do not know why my hon. friend should object to expenditures being made in that section of the country when in other places large sums of money are being expended without any revenue at all to the country.

There are two issues involved. The first one comes from the fact that we are apparently creating a precedent that at some future date may be dangerous. The conditions of high and low water are the same as exist in all rivers where lumbering is carried on. You find the same difficulty in the St. John river where there is the greatest difficulty in getting logs which are cut in one winter down to St. John to saw them the same year. If you come to the rescue of these lumber people on the St. Maurice, will you not have similar demands from the lumbermen on all of the other important lumbering rivers ? They
will ask to be enabled to carry on their industry with similarly favourable conditions to those on the St. Maurice.

Does my hon. friend know that there arp only three rivers under the control of the government; the others are all in the hands of private corporations V The River St. John is not under government control.

The government have control over the River St. John. You will find that we will be asked to vote sums for other rivers besides this. The minister speaks of the revenue to be derived. There is nothing in that argument as this will simply enable that revenue to be derived more quickly ; for the lumbermen must pay the dues sooner or later on every log cut on the head waters of the St. Maurice.

My hon. friend knows there are over 00 miles of navigation in this district on the river and I suppose there can be no objection to the general policy of the government in seeing that the proper dredging is made in that section of the river. It costs us to-day more than $12,000 to do that dredging and it is thought that by this dam that will be avoided. This dam will cost us $100,000 and at 4 per cent that is $4,000 a year, which is a great saving.

The minister has anticipated what I had intended to say in that particular connection. It does not seem to me that the dredging in the stretch above Grande Piles will be discontinued, and therefore that item of $12,000 will not be expended.
